episodes.title: From ₹5L to ₹40L+: The Career Choices That Actually Accelerate Your Salary in the AI Era | FWS
episodes.summary: Sharan discusses how career choices, especially focusing on high‑growth AI and data product verticals, can dramatically accelerate earnings from ₹5 L to ₹40 L+. He emphasizes inspiring leadership, employee‑first culture, and internal transformation over consulting, while also highlighting the slow adoption of AI and the need for CEO compensation to align with transformation success.

learnings.headline: Inspire, don’t manage, to boost productivity
learnings.idea: If you stop trying to manage people and instead focus on inspiring them, you can dramatically increase their output without adding resources.
learnings.why: Shifting from a control‑centric approach to an inspirational one raises employee engagement and accelerates the organization’s “clock speed,” making large teams feel as easy to lead as small ones.
learnings.action: Spend a week designing one simple ritual or story that connects team members to a shared purpose and practice delivering it regularly.
learnings.evidence: "The moment you give up the idea of managing and try finding out how to inspire people, I think you will find managing 200 people or 2,000 people extremely easy."

learnings.headline: Employee‑first, customer‑second drives growth
learnings.idea: Prioritising employee well‑being before customer demands leads to higher engagement and ultimately higher revenue.
learnings.why: When staff feel valued they become more productive and innovative, which creates a stronger value proposition for customers than the reverse approach.
learnings.action: Adopt a policy that measures employee satisfaction weekly and ties a portion of product‑development decisions to those scores.
learnings.evidence: "I have disagreed with it that is the reason I wrote employee first customer second"

learnings.headline: Vertical choice outruns starting salary in tech
learnings.idea: In technology, the initial salary matters little; the career vertical you enter (e.g., high‑growth AI or data products) determines long‑term earnings, while testing or pure coding roles tend to plateau.
learnings.why: Focusing on high‑growth verticals accelerates salary trajectories far more than negotiating a higher entry pay, reshaping how graduates choose their first role.
learnings.action: Map emerging tech verticals in your market and target roles that sit at the intersection of scarcity and strategic importance.
learnings.evidence: "...if you wish to earn high in the technology sector doesn't matter what salary you start what matters is what vertical do you start in if you start in testing you're dead anyway if you start in coding you're dead anyway…"

learnings.headline: Avoid consulting; become a transformer inside industry
learnings.idea: Instead of joining consulting firms, work within a functional area of an industry, propose change, and rise quickly as a change‑maker.
learnings.why: Hands‑on transformation roles provide deeper learning and faster career acceleration than the broad but shallow exposure of consulting.
learnings.action: Identify a company undergoing digital transformation and pitch a pilot project that you can lead from inside.
learnings.evidence: "Don't go consulting because you don't learn anything… be the transformer… be the change maker…"

learnings.headline: Risk‑taking over cost‑cutting preserves morale in recession
learnings.idea: HCL’s “no ATlite left behind” policy kept all staff employed during a downturn, maintaining high motivation and allowing the company to capture market share instead of shrinking.
learnings.why: Retaining talent during a recession protects employee morale and positions the firm to grow when competitors cut staff, turning a crisis into an opportunity.
learnings.action: Create a contingency plan that earmarks a “no‑layoff buffer” budget for critical talent during downturns.
learnings.evidence: "...at HCL we came up with no ATlite left behind… the motivation levels are high… we never saw degrowth in recession"

learnings.headline: AI is in an “ugly duckling” stage, adoption will be slow
learnings.idea: Artificial intelligence is still immature; practical, revenue‑generating use cases will take several years to materialise, much like early electricity or internet adoption.
learnings.why: Expecting immediate ROI from AI leads to misplaced investments; firms should plan for a longer horizon and focus on building foundational capabilities first.
learnings.action: Set a 3‑year roadmap that prioritises data infrastructure and pilot projects before scaling AI across the business.
learnings.evidence: "AI is what I call in an ugly duckling stage… it will happen in 2 years 3 years 4 years and we have to run ahead of that…"

learnings.headline: CEO pay should be tied to transformation success
learnings.idea: Since 90% of CEOs fail to achieve transformation objectives, their compensation should be linked to the achievement of those goals rather than a fixed salary.
learnings.why: Aligning pay with transformation outcomes incentivises leaders to focus on measurable change, reducing the prevalence of ineffective CEOs.
learnings.action: Introduce a variable compensation component that triggers only when predefined transformation KPIs are met.
learnings.evidence: "failure rate of CEOs is almost 90% only 10% of the people are able to achieve the objective of transformation… the compensation is linked with the transformation objective achieved by the CEO"

learnings.headline: Cost‑talk kills Indian IT relevance
learnings.idea: Clients are shifting away from cost‑only discussions toward transformation; IT firms that keep emphasising cost risk losing revenue, growth, and share price.
learnings.why: Understanding the evolving client mindset is essential for IT firms to stay competitive and avoid strategic obsolescence.
learnings.action: Revise sales pitches to highlight transformation outcomes and measurable business impact rather than price reductions.
learnings.evidence: "If you continue talking about the cost, your relevance will go down… your revenue will go down, your growth rate will go down, your share price will go down…"

learnings.headline: Public employee‑run appraisals speed up decision‑making
learnings.idea: An annual, anonymous appraisal of the CEO by all employees, made public, increased organisational speed and clarified managerial roles.
learnings.why: Transparency and collective feedback create accountability and accelerate cultural alignment, leading to faster execution.
learnings.action: Pilot a confidential, company‑wide peer review of senior leadership and publish the aggregated results.
learnings.evidence: "I said if we want to do it, then why don't we open we have a confidential appraisal of mine annually done by one lakh employees and to be made public every year."

learnings.headline: Culture itself is a product innovation
learnings.idea: Innovation is not limited to product pricing or features; it also emerges from building a differentiated organisational culture that aligns with value creation.
learnings.why: Treating culture as a strategic asset expands the sources of competitive advantage beyond technology or price.
learnings.action: Define three cultural pillars that directly support your core value proposition and embed them in hiring and performance metrics.
learnings.evidence: "The innovation is not just in product pricing proposition. It is also in the culture of your organization."
